nd-sos-2026-sl-general-list.title: 2026 General Election Contest/Candidate List (statewide, legislative and judicial contests)
nd-sos-2026-sl-general-list.note: Read through the page's own search, once each for the Statewide, Legislative and Judicial jurisdictions. Only the contest title, office, district, name and party are read, by their headings; the address, e-mail, phone and website columns are never read. The list is alphabetical by family name and gives no ballot order. 4 federal rows (Representative in Congress) left to the federal loader.

nd-sos-2026-sl-primary-list.title: 2026 Primary Election Contest/Candidate List (statewide, legislative and judicial contests), June 9, 2026
nd-sos-2026-sl-primary-list.note: Read the same way as the November list, with the same five columns. Primaries with a field (more names than places): 20; without: 100. Who advanced is read from the November list and checked against the official vote counts.

nd-sos-2026-sl-primary-results.title: 2026 Primary Election (June 9, 2026), official results: state contests
nd-sos-2026-sl-primary-results.note: Election Night Reporting, marked official by the Secretary; statewide totals read from the service behind the page (its Election/GetElectionInfo, Contest/GetContestSearchList and Contest/GetContestResults answers, election 346). Write-in votes count in each primary's total but are not listed; in a two-seat primary a percentage is the share of all votes cast. The date given is the results' last update.

nd-openstates-roster-2026.title: Legislators serving now and statewide officials (the site's own records, from the Open States people project)
nd-openstates-roster-2026.note: Used only to say who holds each seat today and to mark incumbents: names, parties, districts and start dates. Not an official record.

nd-sos-2026-local-general-list.title: 2026 General Election Contest/Candidate List (county offices, soil conservation districts and the Garrison Diversion Conservancy District)
nd-sos-2026-local-general-list.note: Read through the page's own search with the jurisdiction All, which returns every contest in one table (729 rows). Six cells of each row are read, by their headings: the contest title, the office, the district, the county, the name and the party. The address, e-mail, phone and website columns are never read, and only those six cells are kept on disk; the fingerprint is of the answer as it came. Of the 561 county-level rows, 485 name a candidate for an office, 64 name a newspaper (left out) and 12 are contests shown with no candidate; the other 168 rows are statewide, legislative, judicial and federal. The list is alphabetical and gives no ballot order.

nd-sos-2024-general-list-soil.title: 2024 General Election Contest/Candidate List (soil conservation districts only)
nd-sos-2024-general-list-soil.note: The last general election's list, read once through the page's own search with the jurisdiction All. Three cells of each row are read, by their headings (office, district, county), and only the district and county of the soil conservation rows are kept; no name is read, and the contact columns never are. Used to see which county each district was filed under then (a district lies where its candidates live) and whether a district on that list is missing from this year's. local_calendar.t: On November 3, 2026 North Dakota's counties elect their auditor, treasurer, recorder, sheriff and state's attorney (some of these offices are combined, a few counties also elect a clerk of district court, and a county may make an office appointed), the county commissioners whose terms are up, and one supervisor of each soil conservation district; counties in the Garrison Diversion Conservancy District whose director's term is up elect a director, and each county's voters choose its official newspaper. All are no-party offices. Cities and park districts held their regular elections on June 9, 2026, school boards hold theirs each year between April and June, townships elect officers at their annual meetings in March, and Southwest Water Authority directors were on the June ballot, so none of those offices is on the November ballot.

local_coverage.t: Loaded from the Secretary of State's 2026 General Election Contest/Candidate List: 374 county and district contests in all 53 counties (306 for county offices, 56 for soil conservation district supervisors, 12 for directors of the Garrison Diversion Conservancy District in the counties electing one this year) with 485 candidates; 12 of the contests are listed with no candidate. Left out: the 53 contests for a county's official newspaper (64 newspapers, not people) and ballot measures, which a candidate list does not carry; the list has no status column, so a candidate who withdrew is simply absent and cannot be counted. Soil conservation districts do not all follow county lines (McHenry County and McLean County each have more than one; three are shown for a second county that the district's own name names or the 2024 list filed it under), and a voter's ballot carries only the district the voter lives in. The Mouse River Soil Conservation District had a contest on the 2024 list and has no row on this year's; it is named among the gaps. The list is alphabetical and state law rotates names from precinct to precinct, so no ballot order is given; how many commissioners an at-large contest elects is taken from the June 9 no-party ballot, which by law states the number to be elected in November.
local_coverage.s: North Dakota Secretary of State, 2026 General Election Contest/Candidate List; N.D.C.C. 16.1-06-08 and 16.1-11-27 (names rotated), 16.1-11-24 (the June ballot's vote-for number)

measures.t:
Constitutional Measure No. 1
(House Concurrent Resolution No. 3003, 2025 Session Laws, Ch. 614)
measures.q: This constitutional measure would amend and reenact section 9 of article III and section 16 of article IV of the Constitution of North Dakota. The proposed amendment would require constitutional amendments submitted to the electors, by resolution adopted by the legislative assembly proposing a constitutional amendment and each initiative petition and measure proposing a constitutional amendment, to receive an affirmative vote of at least sixty percent of those voting on the question for enactment.
measures.s:
Constitutional Measure No. 1 was placed on the ballot by action of the 2025 North Dakota Legislative Assembly with the passage of House Concurrent Resolution No. 3003 (2025 Session Laws, Chapter 614). If approved, this constitutional measure would amend and reenact section 9 of article III and section 16 of article IV of the Constitution of North Dakota.
The proposed amendment would require constitutional amendments submitted to the electors, by resolution adopted by the legislative assembly and by initiative petition and measure, to receive an affirmative vote of at least sixty percent of those voting on the question for enactment.
measures.sb: The Secretary of State, in the analysis of the statewide measures that North Dakota law requires to be published before the election (N.D.C.C. 16.1-01-07). It is not printed on the ballot.
measures.y: Yes – Means you approve the measure as summarized above.
measures.no: No – Means you reject the measure as summarized above.
measures.f: The estimated fiscal impact of this measure is none.
measures.fb: Printed on the ballot, as the Secretary of State's official ballot language gives it.
measures.r: To pass, the amendment needs more YES votes than NO votes among the voters who vote on it. (North Dakota Constitution, article IV, section 16)
measures.h: Proposed by the Legislative Assembly in House Concurrent Resolution No. 3003 (2025 Session Laws, chapter 614). In North Dakota an amendment proposed by the Legislative Assembly needs a majority of the members elected to each house, on a roll call, before it goes to the voters (North Dakota Constitution, article IV, section 16).
measures.nt: The question shown is the explanation printed on the ballot, from the Secretary of State's official ballot language; the voter then votes YES or NO. The Secretary's mailed measure guide reprints this explanation without the words "proposing a constitutional amendment" after "legislative assembly"; the official ballot language, shown here, has them. The Secretary's guide says a majority vote passes each measure on this ballot.

measures.q: This initiated measure amendment would amend and add a new section to article VIII of the North Dakota Constitution. It would mandate all public school districts, public schools, and public charter schools to provide one breakfast and one lunch each school day to enrolled students at no cost to the student, parent, or guardians. It would allow nonpublic schools, Bureau of Indian Education schools, and other tribal schools the option to provide the same. It would require the State of North Dakota to reimburse school districts and schools at one hundred percent of the current rates used by the state for free meals, and the rate shall be adjusted annually for inflation. It would require the legislative assembly to identify a source of funds for reimbursement and if a source of funds is unable to be identified, reimbursement funds would be appropriated from the legacy earnings fund. This amendment would supersede any other part of the constitution that conflicts with it.
measures.s: Initiated Constitutional Measure No.2 was placed on the ballot by petitions circulated by a sponsoring committee. If approved, it would add a new section to article VIII of the North Dakota Constitution.
measures.sb: The Secretary of State, in the analysis of the statewide measures that North Dakota law requires to be published before the election (N.D.C.C. 16.1-01-07). The analysis goes on to repeat the explanation printed on the ballot, shown here as the question. It is not printed on the ballot.
measures.y: Yes – Means you approve the measure as summarized above.
measures.no: No – Means you reject the measure as summarized above.
measures.f: The estimated fiscal impact of this measure is a $124.3 million to $134.3 million increase in ongoing biennial expenditures for the 2027–2029 biennium and will be adjusted for inflation every year after that.
measures.fb: Printed on the ballot, as the Secretary of State's official ballot language gives it. For an initiated measure the Legislative Council reports the estimated fiscal impact to the Secretary of State (N.D.C.C. 16.1-01-17); its report is linked.

methods: lists

Who is running comes only from the North Dakota Secretary of State’s own lists of candidates for the November 3 general election and the June 9 primary, and the official primary results; each file is named below, with where it was read. The U.S. Senate and House races are on the Congress pages. County and local contests are read from the lists named below too: which local offices are on this ballot, what was read and what is not here yet are set out under County by county, in the words of the notes kept with the lists.
lists

What is read from the lists. The office and the district or place it belongs to, the candidate’s name, the party, the ballot order where the list gives one, the official primary vote counts where they are loaded, and the campaign website where a candidate listed one. Addresses, phone numbers and e-mail in the lists are never read, kept or shown.
lists

Parties. Offices elected on party lines show the party each candidate filed under, written out. Judges and the Superintendent of Public Instruction are on the nonpartisan ballot; the page says so instead of a party. Every county and local contest here is for a nonpartisan office; the page says so instead of a party.
lists

Primaries. Where more people ran in a primary (June 9) than it could send on, everyone on that primary ballot is shown, with who went on to November, read from the general election list. Vote counts are the official results where they are loaded; where they are not, the race says so.
lists
Order. The list is alphabetical and state law rotates names from precinct to precinct, so no ballot order is given. Candidates appear by surname. Never by money, polls or party.
places

Places. A county or local contest is filed under every county it reaches. The names of cities, towns and districts come from the North Dakota Secretary of State, each named among these sources; where something on a county’s ballot could not be shown, that county’s page says what and why.
holders

Who holds a seat today (the Legislature and the statewide offices the roster carries) comes from the Open States roster the record side of this site uses. A candidate matched to a sitting legislator by district and name, one fit only, links to their record page, and their birth date, terms and portrait come from that roster before anything else.
maps

The map and “use my location”. The lines on the map of “your ballot” come from the North Dakota Secretary of State, the North Dakota Legislative Council, the North Dakota Department of Public Instruction and the U.S. Census Bureau: precincts, the districts put together from whole precincts, and the larger districts’ own lines; each source’s own notice is shown with the map. The Legislature’s page draws the Census Bureau’s cartographic boundary files. Your location is used on your own device to find your precinct and is never sent anywhere. The exact spot is not kept: what stays on the device until you tap “Forget” is your precinct with its districts and a rounded copy of the spot (about half a mile). A typed address goes from your device straight to the U.S. Census Bureau’s address finder, only when you press Look up; only the spot it finds comes back, used the same way, and this site never sees or keeps the address. Street pictures are off until you switch them on; then they come from OpenStreetMap’s servers, which see which map squares are asked for. Your county’s sample ballot is the authority on your ballot.
page
Nobody is scored or graded. The cards show the record; the judging is yours.
people

Who the candidates are. For statewide offices, the Legislature, judges and county offices a card may show a photo, an age, the public offices a candidate has held, the government’s own page about an officeholder, the campaign’s website and the headings of its issues page. Official records come first; the rest was found on the open web by one reader and confirmed against the page that states it by a second, and a finding counts only when its source ties the person to this race. Each is labelled by its source and linked to it. Candidates for soil and water, hospital and other small district boards show what they filed and, if they listed one, their campaign website. Never collected, for anyone: home or mailing addresses, phone numbers, e-mail, family, marital status, religion, health, ethnicity, income, employers, schools or legal troubles. No social media profile, people-search site, data broker or voter file is ever a source, and nobody was contacted.
web

Found on the open web. A birth year or an office held is labelled by the kind of page that states it: “according to” a government’s own page or the campaign, “as reported by” Wikipedia or a named news organization. An age from a birth year alone reads “about”, and offices found this way are listed, never added up into years of service. A blank means nothing was found, not that there is nothing.
own

Campaign websites. A candidate’s website is the address they filed with the list, or the campaign’s own site found on the open web and checked against the race it names; the race’s page says which. An address that no longer leads to the campaign is left out.
own
In their own words. The topics a campaign’s issues page lists are shown as headings, with a link to the page; nothing is summarized. Photos from a campaign’s own site are credited to it and linked.
page

The record, not a label. For a nonpartisan office a race’s page shows only what is on the record: a party’s own published endorsement, an earlier run or office under a party label, and the candidate’s own words on their own campaign site, each linked to where it stands. This site never calls a person or a place by a party of its own choosing.
results

How a place has voted. For a nonpartisan office the race’s page shows how the place voted in past partisan elections: the official precinct results, added up here by county and district on the lines in force at that election; the results read here give no figures for a city or township, and the page says so there. It is not a prediction, it says nothing about any candidate or voter, and where very few people voted the split is left out.
polls

Polls of the statewide races are shown only from pollsters in the American Association for Public Opinion Research’s Transparency Initiative, who publish how each poll was done: the latest from up to five of them, each checked against the pollster’s own release, and our own average of the ten most recent, with the arithmetic shown. Polls by other pollsters are counted and named, not shown. A poll is a measure of opinion when it was taken, with a margin of error, not a forecast.
polls

Betting markets. Prices on Polymarket, a prediction market, are shown for the statewide races it lists, as information only: not a poll, not a forecast and not an official record. They are read from its public data, and prices move all day. Where Kalshi or PredictIt (two other markets) lists a race, the page says so and links to it, but shows none of its prices: their terms do not allow other sites to show them. A notice comes before any link to a market. The Civic Archive takes no money from any market and uses no referral links.
lists

The contests for Congress at the top of your ballot are the Congress pages’ own, from the state’s official candidate list: each name as printed, with its party label, in the ballot order the list gives (or by surname where it gives none), with its write-in and incumbent marks. Everything else about those candidates is on their race’s Congress page. Your U.S. House district is found without asking: the whole state is one district.
rules

Ballot questions. Each question’s official texts are shown word for word: the question as it will be printed and, where the record has them, the official summary, what a yes and a no vote do and the fiscal note, each labelled by who wrote it where the record says, and by its source. Where this site puts something in its own words (often the votes needed to pass and how the question got on the ballot), the question’s page says so beside it. Each side’s arguments in the official voter guide are linked, never reprinted.
page

Your ballot, printed or kept. “As it will look” draws your ballot as a printed sample ballot; it is a preview, not an official ballot, and your county’s own sample ballot is the authority. “Keep this ballot on my phone” saves the contests, the names, the questions’ words and the names of your districts and places in this device’s own storage, with the date, to open with no signal. No location, no address and no account: nothing is sent anywhere. “Forget my location and choices” removes it, and so does “Forget this ballot” on the kept page. Anyone holding your unlocked phone can see which districts a kept ballot is for.

changelog.title: Past results: Wisconsin, Minnesota's local races, and every precinct
items: Wisconsin's past results are here: Congress, the Legislature, district attorneys, statewide questions, and Milwaukee and Dane counties' own offices and questions, from the state Elections Commission's official files.

Minnesota now has every local contest of 2020, 2022 and 2024: judges, county offices, cities, townships, school boards, soil and water and hospital districts, and local questions, read from the Secretary of State's own result files (as kept by the Internet Archive after the count was certified) and checked precinct by precinct against the certified results.
Precinct by precinct: on the Past results page, open any county's or contest's precinct table to see each precinct's figures, for the 44 states that publish them. They load only when you open them.

changelog.title: Past results for every state, and the ballot in Spanish (a draft)
items: Past results now cover 49 states and the District of Columbia: the November general elections of 2020, 2022 and 2024, from President down to county offices, cities, townships, school boards, special districts and ballot questions wherever the state or county publishes official figures. Wisconsin's official files are not reachable yet, and the page says so.

Figures are shown by county and by city or town. Where a state's figures come from a compilation rather than its own official count, they are labelled secondary and no winner is marked from them. Where two official records disagree, both are shown and nothing is changed.
Each race page's "This seat before" now finds past elections in every loaded state.

On the draft site only: the ballot pages, menus, Help and the reading settings can be read in Spanish ("¿Leer en español?"). Each translated page says it was translated by Claude, an AI model, and not yet reviewed by a person. Names, office titles as printed and the words on your ballot stay in English; office titles show a Spanish translation beside the official English.
Ballot pages now say in one plain sentence what each office does, at the Beginner and Easy levels, with the official sources one tap away.

changelog.title: Past results: how places and seats voted in 2020, 2022 and 2024
items: New in Election Night: "Past results". Pick a state and a year (the November general elections of 2024, 2022 and 2020), then any contest on that ballot: names and parties as printed, votes and shares, the certified total and where it comes from, a county map, and the figures for each county, city or township.

North Dakota and Iowa are here in full, down to county offices, townships, soil and water districts and every ballot question. Illinois has Congress, the Legislature, judges and the statewide questions; Minnesota has President, Congress, the Legislature, Governor and the statewide offices. Their county and local races are next, and the page says which parts are still missing.

On The Ballot: race pages now have "This seat before", the same seat's past elections, with a note when the district's lines were different then. Ballot question pages have "Questions voters here decided before".
Every figure comes from the state's or county's official certified count and was checked against the official totals. Where two official records disagree, both are shown and nothing is changed.

changelog.title: The dashboard
items: New: a dashboard of the whole record, in three views. "Your place at a glance" shows any state or the whole country: what is on its ballot, who holds its seats, its ballot questions, and a link to its mail-voting facts. "The record, filtered" turns Congress's bills and floor votes into a sentence and charts you can narrow by chamber, topic and year. "Every state, side by side" puts all the states on one map, one measure at a time, with a two-state comparison.

Every figure is counted from the site's records when the page is built, and every chart says where its numbers come from and what they cannot tell you. Places can be compared; people are never ranked.
Beginner shows a few plain tiles; Medium adds the charts; Advanced opens the sources. Each view has its own address and a Share button.
The dashboard is linked from the home page, the menus, the On The Ballot door and Help.

changelog.title: Vote by mail, and questions answered
items: Every state's ballot page now has "Vote by mail or absentee": the last day to ask for a mail ballot and the last day to send it back for November 3, how to ask (the state's own link), how to send it back, what the envelope needs, how to track it, early voting in person, and what the state says for students at school elsewhere in the state or in another state, and for military and overseas voters. Every fact links to the state's own page or law and shows when it was checked. When a deadline has passed, the page says so and points to voting early or on Election Day.
"Your ballot" now says, under the election date, when to ask for a mail ballot.
The Congress ballot pages link each state to its mail-voting facts.

New: On The Ballot's questions page, with plain answers on voting by mail, students, military and overseas voters, moving, checking your registration, finding your polling place, when polls close, early voting, ID, tracking your ballot and a spoiled or lost ballot. Pick your state and each answer uses its own rules.
Every fact comes from the state's own election office or law, or from federal voting sites, and a second check re-read each source. The state election office always has the final word.

changelog.title: Share anything
items: Every part of the site now has a Share button: pages, races, ballot questions, counties, members, bills, votes, maps, the district lenses and Election Night. On a phone it opens your phone's own share sheet. On a computer it offers Copy link, e-mail, Facebook, LinkedIn, X, Bluesky, WhatsApp and Reddit (and text messages on a phone).
Nothing is sent until you pick a place. The place you pick then sees the link. No sharing buttons from those companies are loaded on these pages.
Every race, ballot question and county, down to the local contests, now has its own preview picture, so a shared link shows what it is about.
"Share my ballot" shares your precinct's ballot, after a note saying the link shows roughly where you vote. A shared link never carries your exact location.
The ready-made message sticks to the facts, for example: "U.S. Senate, Minnesota: who is on the November 3 ballot, from the official list."

tax_commissioner.t: North Dakota's tax commissioner runs the state's tax office. It carries out the state's tax laws, such as income, sales, property and oil and gas taxes.
s: About, North Dakota Office of State Tax Commissioner

x.es: El comisionado de impuestos de Dakota del Norte dirige la oficina de impuestos del estado. La oficina aplica las leyes tributarias del estado, como los impuestos sobre los ingresos, las ventas, la propiedad y el petróleo y el gas.

water_board.t: Water district board members run a public district that supplies water, and in some places sewer service or farm water, to its area. They set its rates and budget.
s: What's So Special About Special Districts? (4th ed.), California Senate Local Government Committee

x.es: Los miembros de la junta de un distrito de suministro de agua dirigen un distrito público que suministra agua a su zona y, en algunos lugares, servicio de alcantarillado o agua para la agricultura. Fijan sus tarifas y su presupuesto.
